---
title: "Sleep Confidence Intervals Activity: Code Explainer"
---

This document walks through the key code patterns in the Sleep Confidence Intervals activity.

## Calculating standard error inside `mutate()`

```
sleep_stats <- sleep_stats |>
  mutate(se_hours = sd_hours / sqrt(37))
```

Standard error is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size. This tells you how much uncertainty there is in your sample mean. Note that `sleep_stats` here is a one-row summary table (created by a previous `summarize()`), so `mutate()` adds new columns to that one-row table. You can use `mutate()` on any data frame, regardless of how many rows it has.

## Using `qt()` for the t-distribution critical value

```
sleep_stats <- sleep_stats |>
  mutate(
    t_critical = qt(0.975, df = n - 1),
    margin_error = t_critical * se_hours,
    ci_lower = mean_hours - margin_error,
    ci_upper = mean_hours + margin_error
  )
```

`qt(0.975, df = n - 1)` gives you the critical value from the t-distribution. The 0.975 corresponds to a 95% confidence interval — you want 2.5% in each tail, so you look up the 97.5th percentile. `df = n - 1` is degrees of freedom (sample size minus 1). The critical value is then multiplied by the standard error to get the margin of error.

Each line builds on the previous: `t_critical` feeds into `margin_error`, which feeds into `ci_lower` and `ci_upper`. This works because `mutate()` evaluates columns in the order you write them.

## Selecting specific columns for display

```
sleep_stats |> select(mean_hours, margin_error, ci_lower, ci_upper)
```

`select()` picks which columns to show. This is useful when a data frame has many columns but you only want to display a few for readability.

## Layering annotations on a histogram

```
ggplot(sleep_data, aes(x = hours)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "skyblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = sleep_stats$mean_hours, color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = sleep_stats$ci_lower, color = "blue", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = sleep_stats$ci_upper, color = "blue", linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = sleep_stats$ci_lower, xmax = sleep_stats$ci_upper,
           ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "blue", alpha = 0.1)
```

This chart layers several elements:

1. `geom_histogram()` draws the bars.
2. `geom_vline()` adds vertical lines at the mean and confidence interval bounds.
3. `annotate("rect", ...)` draws a shaded rectangle. `xmin` and `xmax` set the horizontal boundaries (the confidence interval). `ymin = 0` and `ymax = Inf` make it extend the full height of the chart. `alpha = 0.1` makes it nearly transparent so the bars show through.

## Conditional text with `if_else()`

```
meets_cdc = if_else(ci_lower >= cdc_recommendation,
  "Yes - entire CI is at or above 7",
  "No - CI includes values below 7")
```

`if_else()` checks a condition and returns one of two text strings. Here it checks whether the lower bound of the confidence interval is at or above the CDC recommendation. This turns a number into a readable answer.

## Hypothetical scenario with manual values

```
hypothetical_n <- 100

hypothetical_stats <- tibble(
  mean_hours = sleep_stats$mean_hours,
  sd_hours = sleep_stats$sd_hours,
  n = hypothetical_n,
  se_hours = sd_hours / sqrt(hypothetical_n),
  ...
)
```

You can create a tibble with made-up or hypothetical values to see what would change. Here, the activity keeps the same mean and standard deviation but changes the sample size to 100, showing how a larger sample narrows the confidence interval. `sleep_stats$mean_hours` pulls a value from the earlier summary table.

## Common mistakes

**Using `qnorm()` instead of `qt()` for small samples:**

```
# Wrong for small samples — uses the normal distribution:
qnorm(0.975)  # returns 1.96

# Correct for small samples — uses the t-distribution:
qt(0.975, df = 36)  # returns 2.028
```

For large samples (n > 30 or so), `qnorm()` and `qt()` give similar results. For small samples, the t-distribution gives wider intervals, which is more appropriate because small samples have more uncertainty.

**Using 0.95 instead of 0.975 for a 95% CI:**

```
# Wrong — this gives a 90% confidence interval:
qt(0.95, df = 36)

# Correct — 0.975 because you split the remaining 5% between two tails:
qt(0.975, df = 36)
```

A 95% CI leaves 5% total in the tails — 2.5% on each side. So you look up the 97.5th percentile (0.975), not the 95th.

**Confusing standard deviation with standard error:**

```
# Standard deviation — how spread out INDIVIDUAL values are:
sd(sleep_data$hours)  # might be 1.5 hours

# Standard error — how much the SAMPLE MEAN would vary across samples:
sd(sleep_data$hours) / sqrt(37)  # much smaller, maybe 0.25 hours
```

Standard deviation describes the data. Standard error describes the uncertainty in the average. The confidence interval uses standard error, not standard deviation.
